title: Fair or Not?
theme: Fairness and justice: who gets treated how
objectives: I can describe fair and unfair treatment using ten words about justice.
I can explain the difference between equality and equity with a clear example.
I can tell when a statement is a stereotype or a prejudice and say why it is unfair.
I can use the prefixes in-, im-, ex-, and pre- and the ending -ity to understand words.
rationale: The year ends with the vocabulary of fairness, which builds on the power and conflict units and prepares the bias and ethics work of grade 8. The words fall into three groups: fairness at its best (equity, impartial, merit, integrity), unfair beliefs and acts (prejudice, stereotype, discriminate, exclude), and the conditions and responses around them (inequality, tolerate). Equity and impartial are abstract, so the passage anchors them in a concrete selection process that students can picture and judge. Propaganda, oppress, objective, and partial return from earlier units so that students can connect fairness to messages, power, and point of view.

words.def: Fairness that gives each person what they need so that they have a real chance to succeed.
words.ex: The district bought extra books for schools with fewer resources, as a matter of equity.
words.ex2: Equity means a student who needs glasses gets glasses, not that everyone is handed the same thing.
words.nonExample: Giving every student exactly the same help, whether they need it or not, is equal but not always equitable.

apps.academic: Debates about school funding often turn on the difference between equality and equity.
apps.spoken: It's not just about treating everyone the same; it's about equity.
apps.writing: Use equity for fairness that adjusts to what people need, and equality for sameness.

passage.title: The List
paras: The middle school announced a new robotics team with only eight openings, and thirty students wanted one. On Friday, Mr. Dunn posted the list. Amir's name was missing, though he had built the winning circuit at the science fair. Then he overheard a classmate say, "New kids can't handle the hard stuff." That was a stereotype, a lazy picture of a whole group, and it said nothing about Amir's skill.

Amir's friend Lucia told the principal what she had heard. Ms. Torres did not accuse anyone. She asked for the coach's notes and discovered that he had excluded every student who joined the school that year, without testing one of them. "That looks like prejudice," she said, "a judgment made before knowing the facts. Choosing by a label is a way to discriminate against people, even if no one means harm."

Mr. Dunn was embarrassed but honest. Ms. Torres proposed an impartial panel: two teachers and a parent who did not know the students. Everyone would get the same materials and the same time for a building challenge, and the panel would score the results without names. "That is equal," Lucia said, "but some of us have never used these tools."

Ms. Torres nodded. "You are describing equity, giving people what they need so that the contest is truly fair. Otherwise, inequality in who has used the tools before would decide the winners." The school opened the workshop for two extra afternoons. Some students grumbled, but most were willing to tolerate the extra effort once they understood the reason.

The next Friday, the panel posted a new list. Amir was on it, and so were two other new students. Each had been chosen on merit, the quality of their work. Mr. Dunn stood before the team and said, "I made a mistake. People with integrity admit their errors." It took courage, and the team respected him more for it.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "stereotype" most nearly means
choices: a fixed, oversimplified idea about a group
a careful measurement of skill
a prize for the best student
a list of team members
qs.why: The passage describes it as a lazy picture of a whole group that says nothing about Amir's skill.

qs.q: Why does Ms. Torres call the coach's choice prejudice?
choices: He picked students he had tested and found weak.
He wanted to keep the team too small.
He left out new students without testing them, judging before knowing the facts.
He forgot to post the list on time.
qs.why: She says prejudice is a judgment made before knowing the facts, and the coach had excluded new students without testing one.

qs.q: Which detail best shows how the panel stayed impartial?
choices: It had two teachers and a parent.
It scored the results without names, and its members did not know the students.
It chose the same eight students as before.
It met on Friday afternoons.
qs.why: Not knowing the students and scoring without names kept the panel from favoring anyone.

qs.q: Lucia says "That is equal, but some of us have never used these tools." What is she pointing out?
choices: The panel is too small.
The contest is too hard for everyone.
The tools are too expensive.
Treating everyone the same may not be fair if their starting points differ.
qs.why: Her comment leads Ms. Torres to describe equity, which gives people what they need so the contest is truly fair.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Fair choices come from facts, an impartial process, and a willingness to admit mistakes.
Robotics teams should always have eight members.
New students are always better than experienced ones.
Coaches should never choose team members.
qs.why: The story shows the coach's mistake, a fairer process, and his honest admission.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for discussing fairness and unfairness, read a narrative about a team selection that is corrected, practice the prefixes in-, im-, ex-, and pre- and the ending -ity, and write short explanations of fair and unfair choices. The unit asks students to separate beliefs (prejudice, stereotype) from acts (discriminate, exclude) and to see fairness as a process, not only a feeling.

notes.va.equity.n: Distinguish from equality: equal gives the same, equitable gives what is needed. Use a fictional example (shoes sized to each foot) rather than real student circumstances. Keep the word abstract only until the example is clear.
notes.va.impartial.adj: Im- plus partial (from the point-of-view unit). Use sports referees and judges as the anchor. Ask students how a person could stay impartial when a friend is involved.
notes.va.prejudice.n: Prejudge and prejudice share pre- (before); the word means a judgment before knowing the facts. Use fictional cases and avoid asking students to name groups. A person can hold prejudice without meaning harm; the action is what makes it discrimination.
notes.va.discriminate.v: Multiple meaning: unfair treatment (taught) and noticing differences (a trained ear discriminates between notes). Keep the examples about unfair treatment from sounding like real accusations; use invented ones.
notes.va.inequality.n: In- (not) plus equality. Use a simple bar chart of resources to show a gap. Ask students what could narrow it, without prescribing a political answer.
notes.va.merit.n: Link to deserving by quality. Ask students how to measure merit fairly in a contest (clear criteria, blind scoring). Note that who has had a chance to practice also matters, which connects to equity.
notes.va.tolerate.v: Put up with, not agree with. Use small examples (a loud fan) and then larger ones (a different opinion). Distinguish tolerating a difference from tolerating harm: some things should not be tolerated.
notes.va.stereotype.n: Ask students to rewrite a stereotype as a question to test it. Use media examples (movie characters) rather than real groups. Contrast with a generalization backed by evidence about a specific, defined sample.
notes.va.exclude.v: Pair with include; both are common in school rules. Show the difference between excluding someone on purpose and leaving them out by mistake, and how each feels.
notes.va.integrity.n: Abstract: tie it to one specific action students can picture. Integrity is not perfection; it includes admitting mistakes, as Mr. Dunn does in the passage.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The classmate says new kids can't handle the hard stuff. That is a stereotype, a fixed idea about a whole group. When the coach leaves out all new students without testing them, he acts on that idea, and that is discrimination. The principal's panel does not know the students, so it is impartial.'

teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit equity/equality and prejudice/discrimination as contrast pairs after two days and again at one week. Ask students to connect propaganda, oppress, objective, and partial to fairness: who is being treated unfairly, by what message or power, and how would an objective, impartial source describe it.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (equidad, imparcial, desigualdad, estereotipo, integridad, discriminar) not reviewed by a native speaker; check equidad versus igualdad for the equity/equality contrast and desigualdad for the cognate flag.
Sensitive content: prejudice, stereotype, and discrimination are taught through invented, low-stakes school scenarios; a sensitivity reader should check tone and examples.

Sense boundaries: discriminate has a second sense (notice a difference); merit and tolerate have other uses not taught. Equity is taught in its fairness sense, not the financial sense (ownership share).
